threads_text: The companies that control Elvis Presley's songs just sued Anthropic, saying Claude was trained on 274 of them without permission. It is the second music lawsuit against Anthropic this week, after Reservoir asked for up to $151 million over 853 songs. Should AI companies have to pay for every song they train on?
caption:
The companies that control Elvis Presley's music sued Anthropic on October 23, saying Claude was trained on 274 of his songs without permission.
Two days earlier, publisher Reservoir sued over the lyrics of 853 songs and asked for up to $151.4 million.
Anthropic says it disagrees with Reservoir's claims and will fight them.

Should AI companies pay for every song they learn from?

paragraphs.text: A unit of Authentic Brands Group, which controls much of Elvis Presley's intellectual property, sued Anthropic on Friday, October 23, 2026, according to Billboard. Other companies that own rights to Presley's music joined the complaint. The plaintiffs allege that Anthropic used 274 of Presley's copyrighted songs without permission to build Claude, its AI assistant.

The songs named in the complaint include "Can't Help Falling in Love," "A Little Less Conversation," "Don't Be Cruel," "All Shook Up" and "Return to Sender." Beyond training, the suit claims that Anthropic built technology that produces what it calls unlicensed derivative works. Billboard described the case as closely following earlier music industry lawsuits against AI companies.

Richard Busch, the attorney leading the case, said that "The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs." Billboard reported that the filing did not include a specific damages figure, and that Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday, October 24.
A second music lawsuit in the same week

The Presley suit came two days after Reservoir, an independent music publisher, filed its own copyright case against Anthropic in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on October 21, 2026. That complaint, case 5:26-cv-12308, says Anthropic copied the lyrics of 853 compositions that Reservoir owns or controls. Songs cited include Johnny Cash's "Ring of Fire," Madonna's "Papa Don't Preach" and Joni Mitchell's "Big Yellow Taxi."

Reservoir's claims go beyond direct copyright infringement. According to Digital Music News, the complaint also accuses Anthropic of violating the Digital Millennium Copyright Act by circumventing access controls and by removing copyright management information. It states that "Claude has created infringing output for all 853 of the Works, and likely every song in Reservoir's catalog." The publication reported that the complaint relies in large part on The Atlantic's AI Watchdog tool, which lets users search training datasets.

Calculated at the statutory maximum of $150,000 per work, Reservoir's request comes to about $127.95 million for infringement, plus roughly $23.5 million on the DMCA claims, for a total near $151.4 million, according to FourWeekMBA's reading of the complaint. Reservoir also asks the court to order the destruction of unauthorized copies of its songs, including copies in training datasets, internal repositories, model weights and servers. These are amounts the plaintiff is requesting, not damages any court has awarded.

Reservoir filed a separate complaint against the AI music company Suno on the same day. Law Commentary reported that the two Reservoir suits together seek close to $340 million. Busch also represents Reservoir.

Anthropic has said it disagrees with the allegations in the Reservoir case and intends to defend the lawsuit vigorously, according to Law Commentary and FourWeekMBA. The company had not publicly addressed the Presley complaint as of October 24.

The new cases add to a pending dispute over song lyrics. On October 21, Judge Eumi Lee heard arguments over fair use in an earlier lyrics lawsuit brought against Anthropic, and had not ruled as of October 22, FourWeekMBA reported.

Taken together, the filings show music rights holders moving from a few large industry cases toward a wider set of suits from individual catalog owners. Each new complaint relies on the same core question that the earlier lyrics case is testing: whether training a model on copyrighted songs counts as fair use. A ruling in that case would not settle the new suits, but it would give both sides a clearer sense of where courts are leaning.

The remedy Reservoir seeks is also notable. Asking a court to order the destruction of copies held inside model weights goes further than a demand for money, because it targets the trained models themselves rather than only the data used to build them.
The next signal to watch is Judge Eumi Lee's fair use ruling in the earlier lyrics case against Anthropic, which could shape how the Presley and Reservoir suits proceed.
